files.lesson.md: --- order: 17 unit: approx10 node: AC9M10N01 n3 uses: [AC9M10N01 n1, AC9M10N01 n2] assumes: [AC9M8N01 n1] connection: compound-savings title: Rounding over and over summary: "Use a slightly wrong rate once and you're a little out. Use it year after year and the error is multiplied each time, so the gap isn't $4 a year: it's $4, then more, then more." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Say your savings grow at 4.6% a year, and round that to 5% in your head. You'll be nearly right. For a while." --- A saver puts $1000 in an account and leaves it. Each year the bank adds 4.6% of the balance, so the balance is multiplied by 1.046 every year. (The 4.6% is made up; real rates are on the banks' own sites.) She doesn't like working with 1.046, so she plans with 1.05, which is close. ## Predict: ten years on ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a ten-year gap shows who thinks a $4 error stays $4 a year (adding), and who expects it to be multiplied along with the balance." check: type: predict q: "After 1 year the plan with 5% is $4 higher than the real balance. After 10 years, how much higher is it?" options: - "$61" - "$4" - "$40" - "$400" actual: "$61. The real balance is $1000 × 1.046¹⁰ = $1567.89 and the plan is $1000 × 1.05¹⁰ = $1628.89, a gap of $61. It's more than $40 because the extra each year earns extra too." ``` It's only $4 after the first year. Does it stay that small? ## Run: both balances on a calculator ```step stage: run insight: "The balance after ten years is the starting amount times the yearly factor ten times, so the factor is a power." tasks: - check: { type: number, q: "Use a calculator: $1000 \\times 1.046^{10}$, the real balance after 10 years. Give it to the nearest cent.", answer: 1567.89, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "1000 × 1.046¹⁰ = 1567.89." } - check: { type: number, q: "Now the plan: $1000 \\times 1.05^{10}$. What is the gap between the two? Was your prediction right?", answer: 61, tolerance: 0.02, explain: "1000 × 1.05¹⁰ = 1628.89, and 1628.89 − 1567.89 = 61." } ``` ### The real balance ### The plan, and the gap Each year the balance is multiplied by the factor again, so ten years is the factor to the power 10. ## Investigate: why the gap grows ```step stage: investigate insight: "The yearly factor is used again and again, so a small difference between two factors is multiplied in as well. Jin adds the first year's gap ten times." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Work out the gap after 5 years: $1000 \\times 1.05^5$ take away $1000 \\times 1.046^5$. Round each balance to the nearest cent first." answer: 24.12 tolerance: 0.02 explain: "1000 × 1.05⁵ = 1276.28 and 1000 × 1.046⁵ = 1252.16, so the gap is 24.12." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#jin" text: "Jin works out the gap after 10 years from the first year's gap. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: power-times explain: "Line 3: the balance is multiplied by the factor each year, not added to. The first year's gap isn't repeated 10 times: the extra each year earns extra too. The gap after 10 years is $61, not $40." - check: type: question q: "Why is the gap after 10 years more than ten times the gap after 1 year?" options: ["The extra money from the higher rate also earns the higher rate", "The bank makes mistakes", "Rounding always doubles errors", "The gap isn't more: it's $40"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The bank's sums aren't wrong: the two rates are just different.", "Rounding doesn't double errors. Repeated multiplying grows them.", "The gap is $61, which is more than 10 × $4."] explain: "With the higher rate each year's balance is bigger, so the next year's extra is bigger too. Differences grow by the same repeated multiplying as the balances." ``` ### The gap after 5 years Here's how the two balances drift. Notice that the gap isn't the same each year. ```worked 1000 \times 1.046 = 1046 :: Real balance after 1 year. 1000 \times 1.05 = 1050 :: Plan after 1 year. The gap is $4. 1000 \times 1.046^5 = 1252.16 :: Real, 5 years. 1000 \times 1.05^5 = 1276.28 :: Plan, 5 years. The gap is $24.12. 1000 \times 1.046^{10} = 1567.89 :: Real, 10 years. 1000 \times 1.05^{10} = 1628.89 :: Plan, 10 years. The gap is $61. ``` Now try one on paper: the gap after 5 years, the same way. Then type it. ### Find the mistake Read Jin's working. Is the balance added to or multiplied? ### Why does it grow? ## Modify: change the rate ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing the rounded rate shows the gap again grows with the years, can go the other way, and gets large over a long time." tasks: - hint: ["Round 4.6% down to 4%, so the factor is 1.04.", "Use $1000 \\times 1.04^{10}$."] check: { type: number, q: "Round the rate down to 4%. What does the plan say the balance is after 10 years?", answer: 1480.24, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "1000 × 1.04¹⁰ = 1480.24." } smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the yearly factor: with a rate of 4%, what do you multiply the balance by each year? Type it as a decimal.", answer: 1.04, explain: "4% more is 100% + 4% = 104%, so × 1.04." } - hint: ["The real balance after 10 years is $1567.89.", "Subtract the plan from it."] check: { type: number, q: "How many dollars is that plan below the real balance after 10 years?", answer: 87.65, tolerance: 0.02, explain: "1567.89 − 1480.24 = 87.65. Rounding down gives a gap in the other direction, and it's bigger because 4% is further from 4.6% than 5% is." } - hint: ["Use 30 years for both rates, 1.05 and 1.046.", "Then subtract."] check: { type: number, q: "Edge case: the saver plans with 5% again, but for 30 years. What is the gap now, to the nearest dollar?", answer: 468, tolerance: 1, explain: "1000 × 1.05³⁰ = 4321.94 and 1000 × 1.046³⁰ = 3854.34, so the gap is 467.60, about $468. Three times as long, more than seven times the gap." } ``` ### Round down ### How far below ### A long time ## Practise: balances and gaps ```step stage: practise insight: "Working out a balance exactly and with a rounded rate, then the gap between them; the review keeps chopping and rounding separate." tasks: - check: type: number q: "$2000 grows at 3.2% a year. What is the balance after 5 years, to the nearest cent? Use $2000 \\times 1.032^5$." answer: 2341.15 tolerance: 0.01 explain: "2000 × 1.032⁵ = 2341.15." - check: type: number q: "Someone rounds the rate to 3%. What does $2000 \\times 1.03^5$ give, to the nearest cent?" answer: 2318.55 tolerance: 0.01 explain: "2000 × 1.03⁵ = 2318.55." - check: type: number q: "How many dollars is the rounded answer away from the exact one, to the nearest cent?" answer: 22.6 tolerance: 0.02 explain: "2341.15 − 2318.55 = 22.60. This time the rounded rate gives a balance that is too low." - check: type: question q: "Review: a till chops every price to the cent. Compared with rounding, which describes it?" options: ["Its errors all go the same way, so they add up", "Its errors go both ways and cancel", "It is always exactly right", "It only affects the cent"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That describes rounding.", "A chopped price is lower than the exact one.", "Over many sales it adds up to dollars."] explain: "Chopping only ever goes down, so its errors add up." ``` ### The exact balance ### With the rounded rate ### The gap ### Review Chop or round, from the last lesson. ## Make: back to the savings ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the saver: the gap after 20 years is about $195, far more than 20 times the $4 of year one." tasks: - hint: ["Exact: $1000 \\times 1.046^{20}$.", "Plan: $1000 \\times 1.05^{20}$."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A saver plans with 5% when the real rate is 4.6% (both made up). Work out her plan and the real balance on $1000 after 20 years, and how far out she is. Then say how that compares with 20 times the first year's $4." steps: - ["Real: $1000 \\times 1.046^{20} = \\$2458.29$", "the factor, 20 times"] - ["Plan: $1000 \\times 1.05^{20} = \\$2653.30$", "the same, with the rounded rate"] - ["Gap: $2653.30 - 2458.29 = \\$195.01$", "plan minus real"] - ["$20 \\times 4 = 80$, so the gap is more than twice that", "the first year's gap isn't repeated, it's multiplied in"] answer: "195" answerLabel: "Gap after 20 years ($)" tolerance: 0.5 feedback: - ["80", "That's 20 × $4, which is what you'd get by adding the first year's gap each year."] - ["2653.3", "That's the plan's balance. The question asks for the gap."] criteria: - "I worked out both balances with the same number of years." - "I subtracted to find the gap." - "I compared the gap with 20 × $4 and saw it is much bigger." explain: "The plan says $2653.30, the real balance is $2458.29, so she is $195 out: more than twice 20 × $4." - check: type: question q: "What should the saver do to keep her plan close to the real balance?" options: ["Keep the full rate, 1.046, and round only the final balance", "Round the rate to 1 decimal place first", "Round the rate down to be safe", "Use 1 instead, because it's the simplest"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "1.0 is further from 1.046 than 1.05 is: the gap would be bigger.", "Rounding down is just a different error that also grows.", "A factor of 1 means no growth at all."] explain: "Keep the exact factor all the way through and round once, at the end." ``` ### The 20 year gap Back to the saver. Work this out on paper first, then type your answer. ### How to keep it close The rates and balances are made up. Real savings rates are on the banks' own pages and change often. **Also used in** - **Loans and savings.** Compound interest is the same repeated multiplying, so a rounded rate drifts the same way. - **Next lessons.** Exponential relations, where repeated multiplying is the whole idea. ```teacher summary: Students use a rounded rate (5% for 4.6%) in a savings balance year after year, see that the gap grows faster than the first year's $4 because the error is multiplied in each year, and learn to keep exact factors and round once at the end (AC9M10N01, node 3). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can work out a balance after several years with powers. - I can find the gap between an exact and a rounded calculation. - I can explain why the gap grows faster than a fixed amount a year. struggle: "Expecting the first year's error to be repeated, not multiplied. Ask: does the extra each year earn anything?" before: > Do the Run step yourself first. Students need powers on a calculator, and the lesson before (Chop or round?). The one idea: using a rounded value again and again multiplies its error, so the gap grows faster than steadily. The common mistake is adding the first year's gap (Jin's working). The rates and balances are made up: $1000 at 4.6% a year, planned as 5%. Real savings rates are on banks' own sites and change, so none is quoted. No real figures, so no sources. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. $40 comes from adding the first year's gap every year." - "Run: have students enter 1.046^10 and 1.05^10 themselves, and read the gap aloud." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the 20 year gap in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for both balances at the same number of years." - "Modify: before the 30 year edge case, ask whether the gap will be about three times as big or more." stuck: - see: A student says the gap after 10 years is $40. ask: Work out both balances after 2 years. Is the gap $8? fix: "$8.38: the first year's extra $4 also earns interest, so the gap grows faster than $4 a year." - see: A student rounds 1.046 to 1.0 to keep it simple. ask: What does multiplying by 1 do to the balance? fix: "Nothing: no growth at all. Keep 1.046 and round the final answer once." stretch: How many years until the plan with 5% is double the real balance's gap after 10 years? Estimate, then check on a calculator. support: A table with years 1 to 5 for both factors, filled in a row at a time, so the gap column can be seen growing. leads: > Continues AC9M10N01 (node 3). Where it leads: exponential relations (the same repeated multiplying), and modelling growth and decay. exit: q: Does the gap between 1.05^n and 1.046^n times $1000 grow by the same amount each year? Why? a: No. Each year's extra also earns, so the gap grows faster each year. explain: > Money in an account is multiplied by the same factor each year, so after $n$ years it's $1000 \times 1.046^n$. If you round the factor to 1.05, the error isn't added each year: it is multiplied in, so the gap grows faster and faster. Keep the exact factor all the way and round once, at the end. ```

# Jin's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: jin
A saver starts with $1000. The real rate is 4.6% a year, but she plans with 5%.
After 1 year: $1050 against $1046, so the plan is $4 too high.
The gap grows by $4 each year, so after 10 years it is 10 × 4 = $40.
So her plan is only $40 too high after 10 years.
# endregion
